candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'apply it to the poorest or most isolated person' turned a standard hip fracture pathway into a question about who fares worst on it, and 'the first month' pointed to the 30-day outcome in the deprivation data.
candidates.working_title: The same fracture, a poorer area
candidates.core_insight: In England, people from the most deprived areas were more likely to die within 30 days and within a year of a hip fracture than people from the least deprived areas, so an equal pathway can still give unequal results.
candidates.angle: Hip fracture pathways and national standards are designed as one standard for everyone and report the average. The deprivation gap asks what the same pathway delivers to someone who goes home to a cold flat, with no car and no one nearby, and where extra support after discharge would help most.
candidates.position: Hip fracture services should look at their own results by area deprivation and plan extra support after discharge for people from the poorest areas; this is a judgement about fair care, supported by the finding of a gap, not a finding in itself.
claims_needing_evidence: In linked hospital and mortality data for England (2004 to 2011), patients from the most deprived fifth of areas had higher adjusted odds of death at 30, 90 and 365 days after hip fracture than those from the least deprived fifth (Thorne 2016, Osteoporos Int; abstract read; ORs about 1.15 to 1.19, which must not be turned into 'times more likely').
Absolute mortality at 30 days and 1 year by deprivation fifth, needed for an 'N in 100' comparison (Thorne 2016 full text; not in abstract).
Overall mortality in that English cohort was about 9% at 30 days and 29% at 1 year (Thorne 2016; abstract read).
Hip fracture incidence is higher in more deprived areas of England, and the gap persisted over 14 years (national hospital episode analysis; Bhimjiyani 2018, unsure).
People from more deprived areas who break a hip are younger on average (Bhimjiyani 2018 or Quah 2011; to verify).
evidence_leads: Thorne K, Johansen A, Akbari A, Williams JG, Roberts SE. The impact of social deprivation on mortality following hip fracture in England and Wales: a record linkage study. Osteoporos Int 2016;27:2727-2737. doi:10.1007/s00198-016-3608-5 (PubMed abstract read)
Bhimjiyani A, Neuburger J, Jones T, Ben-Shlomo Y, Gregson CL. The effect of social deprivation on hip fracture incidence in England has not changed over 14 years. Osteoporos Int 2018 (unsure)
Quah C et al. The influence of socioeconomic status on the incidence, outcome and mortality of fractures of the hip. J Bone Joint Surg Br 2011 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: In England, people from the most deprived areas were more likely to die in the year after a hip fracture than people from the least deprived areas.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison chart: two bars for 1-year mortality in the most and least deprived fifths of areas, using absolute percentages only if the full text gives them (otherwise a statement card without figures), with a caption line that the link does not prove cause and a short list of questions services can ask of their own data.
candidates.pause: A clear gap in a condition most people assume is treated the same for everyone.
candidates.gain: A reason to ask whether local results are checked by deprivation, and where extra support after discharge could go.
candidates.follow: The account asks who a standard pathway leaves behind, with figures rather than slogans.
candidates.earlier_overlap: None in hip fracture. E010 and E013 address inequality in dementia diagnosis, not outcomes after hip fracture.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find the first question worth asking', seen from a home care worker's first hour after a fall, produced the question that should outlast a normal X-ray: can the person stand and take weight on that leg; 'small print' suggested the report line 'no fracture seen'.
candidates.working_title: A normal X-ray, and still can't stand
candidates.core_insight: When an older person has hip pain and can't bear weight after a fall, a normal X-ray does not rule out a hip fracture; NICE recommends MRI, or CT if MRI is not available within 24 hours.
candidates.angle: Families and care workers hear 'the X-ray is clear' and the person goes home or back to the care home. The question that should outlast the X-ray is whether the person can stand and take weight on the leg. If they can't, the next step is another scan, not reassurance.
candidates.position: A person who can't bear weight on a painful hip after a fall should not be sent home on a normal X-ray alone; MRI or CT should come next, as guidance recommends.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE CG124 recommends MRI when hip fracture is suspected despite negative anteroposterior pelvis and lateral hip X-rays, and CT if MRI is not available within 24 hours (NICE CG124; official guideline, check current wording).

In a meta-analysis of 35 studies of older patients with suspected hip fracture and no definite fracture on X-ray, 39% had an occult fracture that needed surgery on MRI; the rate was 44% in people aged 80 and over (Haj-Mirzaian 2020, Radiology; abstract read). These were patients selected for advanced imaging, so the figure does not apply to every older person with hip pain.
Inability to bear weight after a fall is a recognised reason to suspect hip fracture (NICE CG124 or emergency medicine guidance; to verify).
evidence_leads: Haj-Mirzaian A et al. Use of advanced imaging for radiographically occult hip fracture in elderly patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Radiology 2020;296:521-531. doi:10.1148/radiol.2020192167 (PubMed abstract read; title quoted verbatim)
NICE CG124. Hip fracture: management (2011, last updated 2023)
Jorisal P et al. Umbrella review and meta-analysis of imaging in occult scaphoid and hip fractures. J Clin Med 2024;13:3769 (abstract read; supporting only)
candidates.opening_line_draft: The X-ray was normal, and she still can't put weight on that leg: ask whether she needs an MRI.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card: a drawn X-ray envelope marked 'Illustrative' with the words 'No fracture seen', beside a two-step flow: 'Can they stand and take weight on the leg?' If no: 'Ask about MRI, or CT if MRI is not available within 24 hours.' Source line: NICE CG124.
candidates.pause: Families who have been told 'the X-ray is clear' while the person still can't stand recognise the moment.
candidates.gain: One question to ask and a named next step to ask for.
candidates.follow: Practical questions that change what happens next in care.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E058 says unwitnessed falls can hide fractures in people with dementia; this post is about a normal X-ray and the guideline next step for anyone who can't bear weight.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Change the scale' prompted the move from a score built on thousands of patients to the one person in the bed; the weather forecasting domain suggested the idea of a prediction that describes a group of cases, kept out of the wording.
candidates.working_title: A score for 100 people, used on one
candidates.core_insight: The Nottingham Hip Fracture Score estimates what share of people with a given score die within 30 days; it helps plan care and compare hospitals, but it can't say which person will die, so it should inform conversations and the intensity of care rather than decide whether someone is offered surgery.
candidates.angle: Risk scores move from audit spreadsheets to bedside decisions. Redrawing a score as 100 people with that score shows how many survive even in high bands, and what the score leaves out, such as mobility before the fracture and the person's goals.
candidates.position: A high Nottingham Hip Fracture Score is a reason for senior input and a careful conversation about goals, not on its own a reason to withhold an operation.
claims_needing_evidence: The NHFS was derived in 4,967 patients in Nottingham from age, sex, number of comorbidities, abbreviated mental test score, admission haemoglobin, living in an institution and malignancy, to predict 30-day mortality (Maxwell 2008, Br J Anaesth; abstract read).
Its discrimination in derivation was moderate, with an area under the ROC curve of about 0.72 (Maxwell 2008; abstract read).
Predicted 30-day mortality for each score band, so an icon array can show how many of 100 people in a high band survive (Maxwell 2008 or Moppett 2012 full text).
The score's calibration has been re-examined as overall mortality changed (Moppett 2012 or later validation; unsure).
The NHFS does not include pre-fracture mobility or the person's goals (checkable against the score's variable list).
evidence_leads: Maxwell MJ, Moran CG, Moppett IK. Development and validation of a preoperative scoring system to predict 30 day mortality in patients undergoing hip fracture surgery. Br J Anaesth 2008;101:511-517. doi:10.1093/bja/aen236 (PubMed abstract read)
Moppett IK et al. Nottingham Hip Fracture Score: longitudinal and multi-assessment. Br J Anaesth 2012 (unsure)
Wiles MD et al. Nottingham Hip Fracture Score as a predictor of one year mortality. Br J Anaesth 2011 (unsure)
Marufu TC et al. Prediction systems for mortality after hip fracture surgery: a systematic review (2016, unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: A Nottingham Hip Fracture Score gives the share of people with that score who died within [N to verify] days in the data it was built on; it can't say which of them is the person in front of you.
candidates.visual_idea: Icon array chart: 100 figures for one high NHFS band, with the verified predicted number who die within 30 days marked in burnt orange and the rest in teal, labelled 'predicted from derivation data'; a second panel lists what the score does not include (mobility before the fracture, the person's goals and wishes).
candidates.pause: Practitioners who use the score every day see it redrawn as people.
candidates.gain: A clearer sense of what the number can and can't support in a decision.
candidates.follow: Careful reading of the numbers that shape bedside decisions.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E105 gives UK 30-day and 1-year mortality after hip fracture; this post is about applying a population prediction to one person.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Count something nobody counts' prompted a comparison between what audits record about moving after surgery (whether it happened by the next day) and what they don't (how long the person spends upright each day); the chess clock suggested timing across a whole day.
candidates.working_title: Out of bed once, upright for how long?
candidates.core_insight: Audits record whether a person got out of bed by the day after surgery, but in a Norwegian trial people spent under an hour a day upright on the fourth day after hip fracture surgery, and geriatric ward care increased that time.
candidates.angle: A first-day mobilisation target is a single event. Recovery depends on standing and walking repeatedly through every day, which wards rarely measure. The trial measured it with body-worn monitors and found both the low level and that ward care can change it.
candidates.position: Hip fracture wards should look at how often and how long people are upright each day, not only whether the first mobilisation happened.
claims_needing_evidence: In the Trondheim Hip Fracture Trial, body-worn monitors on day 4 after surgery recorded mean upright time of 57.6 minutes in 24 hours with comprehensive geriatric care and 45.1 minutes with orthopaedic care (Taraldsen 2014, J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci; abstract read).
The geriatric care group also had more upright events and better lower limb function on day 5, with no difference in the need for help to walk (same source).

UK national hip fracture audit measures include mobilisation out of bed by the day after surgery (NHFD key performance indicator; official report, check current wording). No findings of the Scottish Hip Fracture Audit to be stated or implied beyond published reports.
Physical activity stays low in the months after discharge following hip fracture (Fleig 2016 or similar; unsure).
evidence_leads: Taraldsen K et al. Physical behavior and function early after hip fracture surgery in patients receiving comprehensive geriatric care or orthopedic care: a randomized controlled trial. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2014;69:338-345. doi:10.1093/gerona/glt097 (PubMed abstract read)
National Hip Fracture Database annual report, Royal College of Physicians (official document)
Fleig L et al. Sedentary behavior and physical activity patterns in older adults after hip fracture: a call to action. J Aging Phys Act 2016 (unsure)
Davenport SJ et al. Physical activity levels during acute inpatient admission after hip fracture are very low. Physiother Res Int 2015 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Four days after hip fracture surgery, patients in a Norwegian trial spent less than [N to verify] minutes of the whole day on their feet.
candidates.visual_idea: Chart: two horizontal bars each representing 24 hours, one per trial arm, with the verified upright minutes marked in burnt orange and the rest labelled 'lying or sitting'; source Taraldsen 2014.
candidates.pause: A small number set against a 24-hour day.
candidates.gain: A different target for ward teams: repeated upright time through the day, not a single tick.
candidates.follow: Looks behind audit measures at what patients experience.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E118 argues for early mobilisation and E131 that bed rest weakens people; this post shows how little upright time follows even good early care and asks wards to measure it.

candidates.stimulus_use: The chess clock, with two clocks running at once, suggested the two times that start at admission: time to theatre, which is audited, and time without food or drink, which usually isn't.
candidates.working_title: Two clocks start at admission
candidates.core_insight: Fasting guidance allows solid food until 6 hours and clear fluids until 2 hours before anaesthesia, yet people waiting for hip fracture surgery are often kept without food or drink much longer, and again each time the operation is moved.
candidates.angle: Time to surgery is audited everywhere; fasting time rarely is. A person on a trauma list may be 'nil by mouth from midnight', moved down the list, and fasted again, while already undernourished.
candidates.position: Fasting before hip fracture surgery should follow current guidance, food and drink should restart when an operation is postponed, and units should measure fasting time alongside time to surgery.
claims_needing_evidence: European Society of Anaesthesiology guidance allows clear fluids up to 2 hours and solids up to 6 hours before anaesthesia in adults (Smith I 2011, Eur J Anaesthesiol; guideline).

In a Sydney cohort of 92 people having hip fracture surgery in 2023, median fasting was about 11 hours from solids and 11 hours from fluids, and none was offered food or fluid up to the guideline limits (Melton 2025, Nutr Health; abstract read).
Over 40% of that cohort were malnourished on admission (same source).
UK consensus supports offering clear fluids until the patient is sent for theatre ('Sip til send'; unsure, find the published consensus statement).
The Association of Anaesthetists 2020 hip fracture guideline addresses preoperative fasting (Griffiths 2021; full text to check, unsure).
evidence_leads: Melton et al. Pre-operative fasting in a cohort of patients undergoing surgery for fractured neck of femur: a retrospective cross-sectional study. Nutr Health 2025;32:1005-1010. doi:10.1177/02601060251347447 (PubMed abstract read)
Smith I et al. Perioperative fasting in adults and children: guidelines from the European Society of Anaesthesiology. Eur J Anaesthesiol 2011;28:556-569

Griffiths R et al. Guideline for the management of hip fractures 2020: Guideline by the Association of Anaesthetists. Anaesthesia 2021;76:225-237. doi:10.1111/anae.15291 (abstract read; fasting content unsure)
Sip til send consensus statement, Centre for Perioperative Care (2022) (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: In one Australian hospital, no one waiting for hip fracture surgery was offered food or drink as late as fasting guidance allows.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: two parallel timelines from admission to theatre, labelled 'time to surgery' and 'time without food or drink', with the guideline windows (no solids in the last 6 hours, clear fluids until 2 hours before) shaded, and a clearly labelled 'Illustrative example' of a postponed operation showing fasting restarted twice.
candidates.pause: Staff recognise the 'nil by mouth' sign above a bed where the operation is still hours away.
candidates.gain: The guideline numbers and a simple change a unit can make.
candidates.follow: Small practical details with measurable effects on patients.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E102 lists more fasting as one harm of delay and E108 mentions fasting windows in nutrition; this post gives the guideline fasting times and the gap between guidance and practice.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Trace a handover between people or services', from a hospital porter's view, mapped the transfers a person with a broken hip goes through (floor, ambulance trolley, emergency department trolley, X-ray table, ward bed), each of which moves the fracture.
candidates.working_title: Block the pain before the moving starts
candidates.core_insight: A nerve block (an injection of local anaesthetic near the nerves that supply the hip) reduces pain on movement within 30 minutes; because each transfer on the way to the ward moves the fracture, giving it early in the emergency department spares the person pain at every later move.
candidates.angle: Pain is often scored while the person lies still. In the first hours the pain that counts is on movement, and every handover between services involves lifting or sliding the person. Families can ask whether a block has been given; staff can time it before the moves.
candidates.position: A nerve block should be offered as early as is safe in the emergency department, before further transfers, and families can reasonably ask whether one has been given.
claims_needing_evidence: In a Cochrane review of 49 trials, peripheral nerve blocks reduced pain on movement within 30 minutes of placement by the equivalent of about 2.5 points on a 0 to 10 scale (high-certainty evidence) (Guay and Kopp 2020; abstract read).
Nerve blocks probably reduce chest infection and shorten the time to first getting out of bed by about 11 hours (moderate certainty) (same source).
People with dementia were often excluded from the included trials (same source).
NICE CG124 and the Association of Anaesthetists 2020 guideline recommend nerve blocks as part of pain relief for hip fracture (official guideline text; check wording and timing).
A person with a hip fracture typically goes through several transfers between ambulance, emergency department, imaging and ward (descriptive; state as a typical sequence, not a measured count).
evidence_leads: Guay J, Kopp S. Peripheral nerve blocks for hip fractures in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;11:CD001159. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD001159.pub3 (PubMed abstract read)
NICE CG124. Hip fracture: management (analgesia recommendations)
Griffiths R et al. Association of Anaesthetists hip fracture guideline 2020. Anaesthesia 2021;76:225-237 (analgesia section; unsure of exact wording)
Royal College of Emergency Medicine guidance on fascia iliaca block in the emergency department (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: Between the floor at home and the ward bed, a person with a broken hip is moved several times: onto a trolley, off it, onto an X-ray table, onto a bed.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a left-to-right sequence of drawn transfers (floor to ambulance trolley, to emergency department trolley, to X-ray table, to ward bed), each marked 'the hip moves', with a marker showing a nerve block given early in the emergency department and a bracket showing the later moves that follow it; caption gives the Cochrane finding on pain on movement.
candidates.pause: Anyone who has watched the sequence recognises it, and few have counted it.
candidates.gain: Practitioners get a timing argument; families get a specific question to ask.
candidates.follow: Turns pathway detail into care people can ask for.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E106 covers regular pain relief after hip fracture and E186 an illustrative case of opioid relief; neither covers nerve blocks or timing pain relief against transfers.

candidates.stimulus_use: The speech and language therapist's view and 'look at the smallest practical detail' led to the first drink and first meal after surgery, and whether anyone watches the swallow.
candidates.working_title: Watch the first drink after surgery
candidates.core_insight: In one prospective study about a third of older people had swallowing difficulty after hip fracture surgery, so the first drinks and meals are worth watching, sitting upright, for coughing, a wet voice or very slow eating, with a swallow assessment requested if they appear.
candidates.angle: Swallowing problems are thought of as a stroke problem. After hip fracture they are common, easy to miss when the person is lying back or drowsy, and linked with chest infection. The first drink after surgery is a moment when staff and family are both present.
candidates.position: Every older person should be observed at their first drinks and meals after hip fracture surgery, sitting upright, with a low threshold for a swallow screen.
claims_needing_evidence: In a prospective cohort of 181 patients (mean age 83) in an Australian orthogeriatric unit, 34% had oropharyngeal dysphagia after hip fracture surgery (Love 2013, Age Ageing; abstract read).
Dysphagia was associated with existing neurological and respiratory conditions, older age and living in residential care before admission (same source).

Swallowing problems after hip fracture are associated with pneumonia and higher mortality (Byun 2019, BMC Geriatr, unsure; Tsai 2025, Sci Rep, abstract read, single centre, reports aspiration pneumonia as a predictor of mortality).

Signs of swallowing difficulty include coughing or choking on drinks, a wet or gurgly voice after swallowing and slow eating (Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists or NICE guidance; to find).

Byun SE et al. Prevalence, risk factors and prognostic implications of dysphagia in older patients undergoing hip fracture surgery in Korea. BMC Geriatr 2019 (unsure)
Tsai KT et al. Postoperative mortality following hip fracture surgery in older adults. Sci Rep 2025;15:22466. doi:10.1038/s41598-025-06181-9 (abstract read)
Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists guidance on signs of dysphagia (unsure)

candidates.pause: An unexpected link between a hip operation and swallowing.
candidates.gain: Signs to watch at a moment when family and staff are both there.
candidates.follow: Draws on the whole team's expertise, not only doctors'.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Trace a handover between people or services', from an occupational therapist's view, followed a person back from hospital to a care home, where rehabilitation depends on staff who were not part of the hospital plan.
candidates.working_title: Back to the care home, and then?
candidates.core_insight: People living in care homes are often left out of hip fracture care trials; the one trial of outreach rehabilitation in care homes found better mobility at 4 weeks that did not last after the programme ended, which points to rehabilitation that care home staff can continue day to day.
candidates.angle: The Trondheim trial of geriatric ward care excluded people living in nursing homes. Care home residents return with a new fracture to a team that may not have received a rehabilitation plan. The trial aimed at them shows both the gain and how quickly it faded.
candidates.position: People who live in care homes should be offered rehabilitation after hip fracture, planned with care home staff so that practice continues after visiting therapists stop; this is a judgement drawn from a trial whose benefits faded when visits ended.
claims_needing_evidence: The Trondheim Hip Fracture Trial excluded people living in nursing homes (Prestmo 2015, Lancet; abstract read).

In an Adelaide trial of 240 care home residents recovering from hip fracture surgery, 4 weeks of outreach rehabilitation improved mobility at 4 weeks, the mobility gain did not persist, and quality of life was slightly better at 12 months (Crotty 2019, Age Ageing; abstract read).
The trial authors judged the case for funding weak on conventional cost-effectiveness grounds (same source).
A substantial share of people with hip fracture are admitted from care homes (NHFD annual report; official document, to verify).

National Hip Fracture Database annual report (residence before admission; official document)

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Take a common shortcut and qualify it', from a daughter's view in the first minute, led to the familiar request for a relative to 'sign the consent form', and 'permission' pointed to who legally gives consent.
candidates.working_title: Who signs the form?
candidates.core_insight: In the UK, being next of kin does not give you legal power to consent to an operation for an adult; if the person can't decide, the doctors decide in their best interests (or, in Scotland, under the Adults with Incapacity Act) unless you hold the relevant power of attorney or guardianship, and they must still ask you about the person's wishes.
candidates.angle: Relatives are often handed a form or asked 'are you happy for us to go ahead?'. The shortcut hides two things: the family's usual legal role is to inform the decision, not to make it, and the most useful thing they can bring is what the person would have wanted.
candidates.position: Families should be asked what the person would want, and told clearly who is making the decision and on what legal basis.
claims_needing_evidence: In England and Wales, under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, no one can consent for an adult who lacks capacity unless they hold a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare or are a court-appointed deputy with that power; otherwise the treating clinician decides in the person's best interests, consulting those close to them (MCA 2005 and Code of Practice).

In Scotland, treatment for an adult who lacks capacity is authorised by a certificate of incapacity under section 47 of the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000, and a welfare attorney or guardian with relevant powers must be consulted (AWI Act 2000 Part 5 and code of practice).
Northern Ireland provisions under the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 (check what is in force).
GMC guidance requires doctors to take account of the views of people close to a patient who lacks capacity (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).
The Association of Anaesthetists 2020 hip fracture guideline includes a medicolegal section relevant to consent (Griffiths 2021; abstract read confirms the section exists).

Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000, Part 5, and code of practice
Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016
General Medical Council. Decision making and consent (2020)
Griffiths R et al. Guideline for the management of hip fractures 2020. Anaesthesia 2021;76:225-237. doi:10.1111/anae.15291

candidates.visual_idea: Question card: three questions a relative can ask (Who is making this decision? Can she decide for herself if she is given help and time? What do you need to know about what she would want?) with a small footnote naming the relevant law in each UK nation.
candidates.pause: Many relatives assume they are signing, or have been asked to.
candidates.gain: An accurate picture of their role and questions that bring the person's wishes into the decision.
candidates.follow: Explains rights and processes accurately and plainly.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E116 asks families to tell the team who the person was last week; this post explains the legal role of relatives in consent. It borders C09 (capacity), so selection should avoid a near copy there.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Examine a neglected consequence', from a ward clerk's first hour recording next of kin, led to the question an admission rarely records: does anyone at home depend on this person for care?
candidates.working_title: Who is at home waiting?
candidates.core_insight: Many older people are unpaid carers themselves, so a sudden admission with a hip fracture can leave a partner with dementia or a disabled adult child at home without help; asking 'does anyone depend on you?' at admission lets staff arrange cover the same day.
candidates.angle: Admission paperwork records who to contact about the patient, not who relies on the patient. A hip fracture is a sudden, unplanned admission, so the second question becomes urgent within hours.
candidates.position: Every emergency admission of an older person should include the question 'Does anyone depend on you for care?', with a same-day route to social work when the answer is yes.
claims_needing_evidence: A substantial number of people aged 65 and over provide unpaid care, including people aged 80 and over (Census 2021 England and Wales, ONS; Scotland's Census 2022, National Records of Scotland; official statistics).
In Scotland, adult carer support plans include emergency and future care planning (Carers (Scotland) Act 2016; unsure of section).
There are no data on how many hip fracture patients are themselves carers; the post must not state a frequency among hip fracture patients.

candidates.opening_line_draft: When an older person is admitted with a broken hip, staff record who to contact; the question to add is whether anyone at home depends on them.
candidates.visual_idea: Illustration: a drawn admission form, labelled 'Illustrative', with the next-of-kin box filled in and an added line 'Does anyone depend on you for care? Who, and who is with them now?', annotated with where a 'yes' should go that day.
candidates.pause: Older carers and their families recognise the fear at once.
candidates.gain: A question patients or relatives can raise straight away, and one staff can add to clerking.
candidates.follow: Notices people who fall between services.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Take a common shortcut and qualify it', from a doctor in training writing the discharge prescription, pointed to opioids copied from the inpatient chart onto the discharge list without a plan to reduce them.
candidates.working_title: An opioid at discharge needs an end date
candidates.core_insight: Opioids started for hip fracture pain should leave hospital with a short supply, a written plan to reduce and stop, a laxative and a named person to review them, because most people's pain lessens as they recover while the harms of continued use (constipation, drowsiness, falls) remain.
candidates.angle: The discharge prescription is often a copy of the inpatient chart. A short list of four items turns it into a plan. The plan also needs a route back for the minority whose pain persists, so the answer is review, not an automatic stop.
candidates.position: Every opioid on a hip fracture discharge prescription should come with a written reduction plan and a review date.
claims_needing_evidence: An international multidisciplinary consensus recommends short-course opioids at discharge after surgery, with a tapering plan and communication to primary care (Levy 2021, Anaesthesia; full text to read).
Some older people are still taking opioids months after hip fracture surgery (national cohort data, e.g. Denmark; unsure).

In the HEALTH trial, about 1 in 10 people reported moderate to severe pain 1 and 2 years after arthroplasty for femoral neck fracture, so some need continued review (Noori 2020, J Orthop Trauma; abstract read).
Opioids are associated with falls and constipation in older people (systematic review or national guidance; to find).

candidates.working_title: Deciding about a care home in week two
candidates.core_insight: Recovery after hip fracture continues for many months, with leg function taking close to a year to reach its best in a large study, so a decision about a permanent move to a care home made in the first weeks may rest on the person at their weakest.
candidates.angle: The acute ward is where a person looks least capable. Asking 'could she manage at home?' in week two answers a question about month six with evidence from week two. Sometimes a care home is the right choice; the question is when to decide and whether the person has had the chance to recover.
candidates.position: Where it is safe and possible, a decision about permanent care home placement after hip fracture should wait until the person has had time and rehabilitation to recover, with the person central to the decision.
claims_needing_evidence: In a Baltimore cohort of 674 community-dwelling people with hip fracture (1990 to 1991), time to maximum recovery ranged from about 4 months for mood, arm function and thinking to about 11 months for leg function (Magaziner 2000; abstract read).

UK discharge guidance recommends that decisions about long-term care are not normally made in an acute hospital (NHS England hospital discharge guidance or NICE NG27; exact wording to find in an official document; unsure).
Rehabilitation after hip fracture increases the chance of returning home (Cochrane review of multidisciplinary rehabilitation, Handoll 2021; unsure).

candidates.working_title: The patients hip fracture trials leave out
candidates.core_insight: People with dementia make up a large share of people with hip fracture, yet many hip fracture trials exclude them, so results may apply poorly to many of the patients clinicians treat; UK law allows research inclusion with consultee advice.
candidates.angle: Consent processes designed for planned research fit badly with an emergency operation within a day or so. The result is evidence built on the more able patients and applied to everyone. Checking the exclusion list is a reading habit worth teaching.
candidates.position: Hip fracture trials should include people with dementia by default, using the established consultee arrangements, and readers should check exclusion criteria before applying results to their patients.
claims_needing_evidence: In the FAITH and HEALTH trials, dementia or cognitive impairment accounted for 22% and 36% of exclusions respectively (Hebert-Davies 2012, Injury; abstract read).
In the hip fracture studies reviewed, dementia prevalence averaged about 28%, with a range of 2% to 51% (same source).
A Cochrane review of nerve blocks for hip fracture reports that people with dementia were often excluded from the included trials (Guay and Kopp 2020; abstract read).

candidates.core_insight: In most of 19 countries and regions studied, the age- and sex-standardised rate of hip fracture fell between 2005 and 2018, but because more people are living into their 80s and 90s the yearly number of hip fractures is projected to nearly double by 2050.
candidates.angle: Headlines say hip fractures are rising or falling depending on which figure they use. Both can be true: one figure describes a person's risk at a given age, the other how many beds, operations and rehabilitation places will be needed.
candidates.position: A falling rate is good news for individuals and no reason to plan for fewer hip fractures.
claims_needing_evidence: Across 19 countries and regions (2005 to 2018), age- and sex-standardised hip fracture incidence decreased in most countries (Sing 2023, J Bone Miner Res; abstract read).
The projected annual number of hip fractures nearly doubles from 2018 to 2050 (same source).
The UK trend in standardised incidence within that study (full text).
Ageing of the population explains the rising count despite falling rates (same source; check the authors' explanation).

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Take a common shortcut and qualify it', from a paramedic's view with 'tuning' as the process, led to the prescribing rule 'start low, go slow' and its missing third part: keep increasing until the pain is controlled.
candidates.working_title: Start low, go slow, and keep going
candidates.core_insight: Older people with hip fracture need lower starting doses of opioids and frequent review, but doses then need increasing until pain on movement is controlled; in a US study people with advanced dementia received about a third of the opioid given to cognitively intact patients, while an orthogeriatric unit using a standard protocol found no such gap.
candidates.angle: 'Start low, go slow' is taught as caution. Applied without the next step, it becomes one small dose and a long wait, and the people least able to ask for more receive least. A written protocol with regular reassessment removes the reliance on asking.
candidates.position: Pain relief for hip fracture should follow a written protocol with regular reassessment of pain on movement, using an observational pain tool for people who can't report pain, so the dose follows the person's pain.
claims_needing_evidence: In a prospective US cohort, patients with hip fracture and advanced dementia received about one third of the morphine-equivalent dose given to cognitively intact patients, and 83% of cognitively intact patients had no standing analgesic order (Morrison and Siu 2000, J Pain Symptom Manage; abstract read). Old US data: the post must say so.

In a French orthogeriatric unit with standardised pain management, preoperative strong opioid doses did not differ by cognitive status (Ruel 2021, BMC Geriatr; abstract read; small retrospective study).
NICE CG124 recommends assessing pain on arrival, within 30 minutes of giving pain relief and regularly, including in people with cognitive impairment (NICE CG124; check wording).
Emergency department pain treatment for older people with hip fracture is often delayed (Hwang 2006, J Am Geriatr Soc; unsure).

candidates.working_title: Which abilities come back first
candidates.core_insight: After a hip fracture, different abilities recover at different speeds: in a large study, mood, arm function and thinking reached their best in about 4 months while leg function took close to a year, and many people did not regain their earlier level for tasks such as stairs.
candidates.angle: Families often hear about the weeks a bone takes to heal. The more useful timeline is ability by ability: what to expect back by 4 months, what can keep improving to a year, and what may need equipment or help.
candidates.position: People should be given a realistic, ability-by-ability recovery timeline at discharge, and rehabilitation and follow-up should run long enough to match how long walking takes to recover.
claims_needing_evidence: In a Baltimore cohort of 674 community-dwelling people with hip fracture followed for 2 years, time to maximum recovery was about 3.9 months for depressive symptoms, 4.3 months for upper limb function, 4.4 months for cognition and 11.2 months for lower limb function (Magaziner 2000; abstract read).

Among people who managed each task without help before the fracture, new dependence ranged from about 20% for putting on trousers to about 90% for climbing five stairs (same source; the time point needs the full text).
Across studies, a substantial proportion of people do not regain their pre-fracture level of walking (Dyer 2016, BMC Geriatr review; unsure).
The cohort was recruited in 1990 to 1991; recovery may differ with current care (limitation to state).

candidates.working_title: Fast enough, and faster
candidates.core_insight: Observational studies link delays beyond about a day or two with more deaths after hip fracture, but the HIP ATTACK trial found that surgery within about 6 hours did not reduce deaths or major complications compared with standard care at a median of about 24 hours.
candidates.angle: Both findings can be true because they answer different questions. Removing avoidable delay (waiting for a theatre slot, or for tests that won't change management) is worth doing; racing to operate within hours has not been shown to save lives.
candidates.position: The aim for hip fracture surgery is to remove avoidable delay, operating on the day of or the day after admission, rather than to operate as fast as physically possible.
claims_needing_evidence: In HIP ATTACK (2,970 patients, 69 hospitals, 17 countries), median time to surgery was 6 hours with accelerated surgery and 24 hours with standard care; 90-day deaths were 9% and 10%, and major complications 22% in both groups (Borges 2020, Lancet; abstract read).
In a large Ontario cohort, waiting more than 24 hours was associated with higher 30-day mortality (Pincus 2017, JAMA; unsure).
NICE CG124 recommends surgery on the day of, or the day after, admission (NICE CG124; check wording).
The standard-care median of 24 hours is faster than many hospitals achieve, so the trial compared very fast with fast (interpretation; check trial discussion).

candidates.working_title: Spinal or general: what the big trial found
candidates.core_insight: In a trial of 1,600 older adults having hip fracture surgery, spinal and general anaesthesia gave similar results for walking and survival at 60 days, so the choice can follow the person's preferences and the anaesthetist's assessment of their particular risks.
candidates.angle: Families often hear that one type of anaesthetic is 'safer' for older people. A large trial found no clear difference in walking or survival two months later, which lets the conversation turn to the person's preferences and specific risks.
candidates.position: People with hip fracture and their families can ask for the anaesthetic choice to be explained and their preferences included, since neither option has shown a clear advantage for walking or survival.
claims_needing_evidence: In REGAIN (1,600 previously ambulatory patients aged 50 and over, 46 US and Canadian hospitals), death or inability to walk about 3 metres independently at 60 days occurred in 18.5% with spinal and 18.0% with general anaesthesia; deaths within 60 days were 3.9% and 4.1% (Neuman 2021, N Engl J Med; abstract read).
About 16% of those assigned to spinal anaesthesia received general anaesthesia instead (same source; affects interpretation).
A Chinese trial (RAGA) also found no clear difference between regional and general anaesthesia in its main outcome (Li 2022, JAMA; unsure).
Trial exclusions, to state who the result may not apply to (REGAIN full text).

candidates.working_title: Partial weight-bearing is an instruction few older people can follow
candidates.core_insight: In a gait study, none of 16 patients aged 75 or over could keep to a partial weight-bearing limit after hip fracture surgery, and in a large US dataset restricted weight-bearing was linked with more complications, so surgery for older people should aim to allow full weight-bearing from the start.
candidates.angle: Restricted weight-bearing is written as a safety measure. For most older people it means either not walking at all or walking in breach of the instruction, and neither is what the surgeon intended.
candidates.position: Hip fracture surgery in older adults should be planned so the person can bear weight as tolerated; any restriction should be an exception with a stated reason and a plan for how the person will move.
claims_needing_evidence: Using insole force sensors, none of 16 patients aged 75 and over after hip fracture surgery kept to a 20 kg partial weight-bearing limit, 69% exceeded it more than twofold, while most younger ankle fracture patients complied (Kammerlander 2018, J Bone Joint Surg Am; abstract read).

In 4,918 patients over 60 in the 2016 NSQIP hip fracture dataset, restricted weight-bearing was associated with higher adjusted odds of adverse events and 30-day mortality (Ottesen 2018, Bone Joint J; abstract read; observational, so 'linked with').
UK standards recommend that hip fracture surgery should allow full weight-bearing (BOAST or NICE CG124; unsure, check wording).

candidates.working_title: Transfusion after hip fracture surgery: symptoms first
candidates.core_insight: In the FOCUS trial of 2,016 people after hip fracture surgery who had heart disease or its risk factors, transfusing to keep haemoglobin above 100 g/L did not improve survival or walking at 60 days compared with transfusing for symptoms or a haemoglobin below 80 g/L.
candidates.angle: The trial's main outcome was whether people could walk across a room without help at 60 days, an outcome patients value, and the restrictive group received a median of no transfusions.
candidates.position: After hip fracture surgery, a restrictive approach to transfusion (for symptoms, or haemoglobin below 80 g/L) is appropriate for most older people, including many with cardiovascular disease.
claims_needing_evidence: In FOCUS, death or inability to walk across a room without human help at 60 days occurred in 35.2% with a liberal threshold (100 g/L) and 34.7% with a restrictive strategy (symptoms or below 80 g/L); a median of 2 units was given in the liberal group and none in the restrictive group; 60-day deaths were 7.6% and 6.6% (Carson 2011, N Engl J Med; abstract read).
Participants were aged 50 or over with a history of, or risk factors for, cardiovascular disease and haemoglobin below 100 g/L after surgery (same source).
UK transfusion guidance recommends restrictive thresholds (NICE NG24; unsure of exact thresholds).
People with acute coronary syndrome were outside this question and may need different thresholds (MINT trial, Carson 2023; unsure).

candidates.working_title: What should and shouldn't hold up hip fracture surgery
candidates.core_insight: Guidance lists a short set of problems worth correcting before hip fracture surgery (such as marked anaemia, anticoagulant effect, dehydration, electrolyte problems, uncontrolled diabetes or heart failure, a correctable arrhythmia or a chest infection), while antiplatelet drugs and waiting for an echocardiogram are not usually reasons to delay.
candidates.angle: Delays attributed to 'medically unfit' often turn out to be waits for a test or for a drug to wear off that guidance says need not delay surgery. Knowing the short list helps a junior doctor ask what exactly is being corrected and by when.
candidates.position: Hip fracture surgery should not be delayed for antiplatelet drugs or routine echocardiography; any delay should name the specific correctable problem and when it will be corrected.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE CG124 lists correctable comorbidities that can justify delaying surgery: anaemia, anticoagulation, volume depletion, electrolyte imbalance, uncontrolled diabetes, uncontrolled heart failure, correctable cardiac arrhythmia or ischaemia, acute chest infection and exacerbation of chronic chest conditions (NICE CG124; check exact wording).
The Association of Anaesthetists 2020 guideline advises that surgery should not be delayed for patients taking antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel (Griffiths 2021; full text to check).
The same guideline advises that echocardiography should not delay surgery (full text to check; the abstract lists echocardiography among areas of controversy).
Direct oral anticoagulants: timing of surgery depends on the drug, dose and kidney function (same guideline; check).

candidates.working_title: When an operation may not be the kindest choice
candidates.core_insight: For most people who break a hip, including many with dementia, surgery gives the best pain relief; for a small group of very frail care home residents near the end of life, a Dutch study found that choosing not to operate, after shared decision-making and with good palliative care, gave similar quality of life in the following weeks, although most of those people died within 30 days.
candidates.angle: The choice is often framed as 'operate or do nothing'. Care without an operation is active care: pain relief, positioning, nursing and support through dying. It deserves open discussion for the few people for whom surgery is unlikely to add good time, and it is no default for anyone because they are old or frail.
candidates.position: For a very frail person near the end of life, families and clinicians should be able to discuss care without an operation as a legitimate choice, while surgery remains the usual recommendation for almost everyone else because it relieves pain best.
claims_needing_evidence: In FRAIL-HIP (172 frail, institutionalised people aged 70 and over with limited life expectancy, 25 Dutch hospitals), 88 chose non-operative and 84 operative management after shared decision-making; proxy-rated quality of life in the non-operative group stayed within the prespecified non-inferiority margin; 30-day mortality was 83% without and 25% with an operation; 51% of proxies rated the quality of dying as good to almost perfect (Loggers 2022, JAMA Surg; abstract read). Not randomised: groups chose.
Eligibility required frailty markers (malnutrition or cachexia, ASA grade IV or V, or severe mobility limitation) and institutional residence (same source).
Guidelines recommend surgery for most people with hip fracture, including for pain relief (NICE CG124; Association of Anaesthetists 2020; check wording).
evidence_leads: Loggers SAI et al. Evaluation of quality of life after nonoperative or operative management of proximal femoral fractures in frail institutionalized patients: the FRAIL-HIP study. JAMA Surg 2022;157:424-434. doi:10.1001/jamasurg.2022.0089 (PubMed abstract read)
NICE CG124. Hip fracture: management
Griffiths R et al. Association of Anaesthetists hip fracture guideline 2020. Anaesthesia 2021;76:225-237
candidates.opening_line_draft: For most people who break a hip, an operation is the best way to control the pain; for a few people close to the end of life, it may not be.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison: two columns, 'Operation' and 'Care without an operation', listing what each involves (pain relief, nursing, positioning, support for the family) and the FRAIL-HIP findings in plain words, with a clear note: 'A small, selected group of very frail care home residents; not a randomised trial'.
candidates.pause: Families facing this decision rarely see it discussed openly.
candidates.gain: Permission to ask about both options and an accurate picture of each.
candidates.follow: Takes hard decisions seriously, avoiding both abandonment and burdensome treatment.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E124 argues frailty should not become 'do not bother'; this post keeps that position and adds the narrow case in which not operating may serve the person's goals.

candidates.working_title: A geriatric ward improved walking at four months
candidates.core_insight: In the Trondheim trial, people aged 70 and over with hip fracture admitted directly to comprehensive geriatric care on a dedicated ward had better mobility four months later than those given usual orthopaedic care.
candidates.angle: Orthogeriatric care is usually argued for on mortality or length of stay. This trial measured mobility at four months, an outcome people value, and found a benefit; the same trial showed more time upright in the first days.
candidates.position: Older people with hip fracture should be cared for in an orthogeriatric model that includes comprehensive geriatric assessment, and services should measure mobility months later, not only in-hospital results.
claims_needing_evidence: 397 home-dwelling patients aged 70 and over who could walk 10 m before the fracture were randomised; mean Short Physical Performance Battery at 4 months was 5.12 with comprehensive geriatric care and 4.38 with orthopaedic care (difference 0.74) (Prestmo 2015, Lancet; abstract read).
The trial excluded nursing home residents and people under 70 (same source).
What the geriatric ward care included (full text).
What a difference of about 0.7 points on the SPPB means in practice (Perera 2006, J Am Geriatr Soc, on meaningful change; unsure).
Reported cost-effectiveness (Prestmo 2015 full text).
evidence_leads: Prestmo A et al. Comprehensive geriatric care for patients with hip fractures: a prospective, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet 2015;385:1623-1633. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(14)62409-0 (PubMed abstract read)
Taraldsen K et al. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2014;69:338-345 (same trial; abstract read)
Perera S et al. Meaningful change and responsiveness in common physical performance measures in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc 2006 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: A Norwegian trial compared two kinds of hospital care after hip fracture by measuring how well people could move four months later.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: two drawn pathways from the emergency department, one to a geriatric ward with a team (doctor, nurse, physiotherapist, occupational therapist) and one to an orthopaedic ward, ending at 'mobility at 4 months' with the verified SPPB means and a plain note of what the scale tests (balance, walking speed, rising from a chair).
candidates.pause: A clear example of good care with a result patients value.
candidates.gain: Evidence for asking about orthogeriatric care, and a sense of what it includes.
candidates.follow: Shows models of care that work, not only failures.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E103 argues for orthogeriatric co-management in general; this post reports a specific trial with a mobility outcome at four months.

candidates.working_title: A person whose job is to help people eat
candidates.core_insight: In a Cardiff trial of women with hip fracture, adding dietetic assistants (staff whose job was to help patients choose, get and eat food) increased daily energy intake, and fewer women died on the trauma ward and by four months.
candidates.angle: Nutrition after hip fracture is often framed as supplements to prescribe. This trial tested a person with time for mealtimes, and it changed how much patients ate.
candidates.position: Hip fracture wards should have staff with protected time to help people eat, because food helps only when it is eaten.
claims_needing_evidence: In an open randomised trial of 318 women with hip fracture on one acute trauma ward, those supported by dietetic assistants were less likely to die on the ward (4.1% versus 10.1%) and by 4 months (13.1% versus 22.9%), and had higher mean energy intake (1,105 versus 756 kcal a day) (Duncan 2006, Age Ageing; abstract read).
Limitations: single centre, open design, women only, conducted about two decades ago (same source; state plainly).
Wider evidence on nutritional supplementation after hip fracture is of low certainty (Avenell 2016, Cochrane; unsure).
evidence_leads: Duncan DG, Beck SJ, Hood K, Johansen A. Using dietetic assistants to improve the outcome of hip fracture: a randomised controlled trial of nutritional support in an acute trauma ward. Age Ageing 2006;35:148-153. doi:10.1093/ageing/afj011 (PubMed abstract read)
Avenell A et al. Nutritional supplementation for hip fracture aftercare in older people. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016 (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: One trial on a hip fracture ward tested a simple change: give someone the job of helping patients eat.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison chart: daily energy intake in the two groups (verified kcal), and deaths on the ward and by four months as natural frequencies per 100 women, with a caption noting one hospital and women only.
candidates.pause: A simple human change with a large measured difference.
candidates.gain: A concrete model to ask for or to build.
candidates.follow: Examples of good care with evidence behind them.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E108 says nutrition after hip fracture is treatment; this post adds a tested staffing model.

candidates.working_title: Cemented half hip replacement: the trial that measured quality of life
candidates.core_insight: In the UK WHiTE 5 trial of 1,225 people aged 60 and over, cemented hemiarthroplasty gave modestly better quality of life at 4 months and fewer fractures around the implant than uncemented hemiarthroplasty, with no clear difference in deaths at 12 months.
candidates.angle: The debate about cement has centred on a rare reaction during surgery. The trial measured what patients experienced in the following months and found a small benefit in favour of cement.
candidates.position: For most older people having a hemiarthroplasty, a cemented implant is the better-supported choice.
claims_needing_evidence: Mean EQ-5D utility at 4 months was 0.371 with cemented and 0.315 with uncemented hemiarthroplasty (adjusted difference 0.055, within the stated minimal important difference range of 0.050 to 0.075); periprosthetic fractures 0.5% versus 2.1%; 12-month mortality 23.9% versus 27.8%, not a clear difference; 4-month follow-up data for 71.6% (Fernandez 2022, N Engl J Med; abstract read).
Cemented implants were cost-saving with slightly more quality-adjusted life years (Png 2022, Bone Joint J; abstract read).
NICE CG124 recommends cemented implants for hemiarthroplasty (check wording).
Whether the trial included people who lacked capacity through consultee agreement (full text; unsure).
evidence_leads: Fernandez MA et al. Cemented or uncemented hemiarthroplasty for intracapsular hip fracture. N Engl J Med 2022;386:521-530. doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2108337 (PubMed abstract read)

Png ME et al. Cost-utility analysis of cemented hemiarthroplasty versus hydroxyapatite-coated uncemented hemiarthroplasty (WHiTE 5). Bone Joint J 2022;104-B:922-928. doi:10.1302/0301-620X.104B8.BJJ-2022-0417.R1 (abstract read)
NICE CG124. Hip fracture: management
candidates.opening_line_draft: A UK trial of [N to verify] people compared cemented and uncemented half hip replacements by measuring quality of life four months later.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison: two bars for EQ-5D at 4 months with the minimal important difference range shaded, and icon arrays per 1,000 people for fractures around the implant (5 and 21), labelled; the mortality result stated in words as 'no clear difference'.
candidates.pause: Practitioners familiar with the cement debate see a direct result on patient-reported outcomes.
candidates.gain: Accurate figures for explaining the choice.
candidates.follow: Reads trials by the outcomes patients value.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Rehabilitation after hip fracture can work with dementia
candidates.core_insight: In a Finnish trial, people with mild or moderate dementia who received intensive geriatric rehabilitation after hip fracture were more often living independently three months later than those who did not, so dementia alone should not exclude someone from rehabilitation, even though the overall evidence is limited.
candidates.angle: People with dementia are often judged unable to benefit because they may not remember the exercises. Trial subgroups suggest many can gain, and the practical question becomes how to adapt rehabilitation (repetition, familiar staff, family involvement).
candidates.position: People with dementia should be offered rehabilitation after hip fracture, adapted to their needs, rather than being excluded because of the diagnosis.
claims_needing_evidence: In a preplanned subgroup analysis of a Finnish trial of 243 independently living patients aged 65 and over, 91% of those with mild dementia in the intervention group were living independently at 3 months versus 67% of controls, and 63% versus 17% of those with moderate dementia (numbers small: 24 and 12 in the moderate groups); there was no difference for severe dementia (Huusko 2000, BMJ; abstract read).
A 2020 Cochrane review found 7 trials (555 participants) with low or very low certainty evidence, none designed specifically for people with dementia (Smith 2020, Cochrane; abstract read).
People with dementia can improve movement through repeated practice even without remembering the teaching (other category C02-21 source; check before cross-reference).
evidence_leads: Huusko TM et al. Randomised, clinically controlled trial of intensive geriatric rehabilitation in patients with hip fracture: subgroup analysis of patients with dementia. BMJ 2000;321:1107-1111. doi:10.1136/bmj.321.7269.1107 (PubMed abstract read; PMC full text available)

Smith TO et al. Enhanced rehabilitation and care models for adults with dementia following hip fracture surgery. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;2:CD010569. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD010569.pub3 (abstract read)
Allen J et al. Effectiveness of rehabilitation for people with dementia after hip fracture: systematic review (unsure)
candidates.opening_line_draft: People with mild or moderate dementia gained from intensive rehabilitation after a broken hip in a Finnish trial.
candidates.visual_idea: Chart: bars as natural frequencies for people with mild and with moderate dementia living independently at 3 months, with and without intensive rehabilitation, with group sizes printed and a label 'subgroup of one trial; small numbers'.
candidates.pause: A common assumption met with concrete figures.
candidates.gain: Grounds to ask for rehabilitation for a relative with dementia.
candidates.follow: Evidence about people who are often left out.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E023 argues age is no reason not to diagnose and E134 questions 'too frail for rehab'; neither covers rehabilitation after hip fracture for people with dementia.

candidates.working_title: After a fall, knee pain can come from the hip
candidates.core_insight: Pain from the hip joint can be felt in the thigh or knee, so an older person with new knee pain after a fall, especially one who can't bear weight, needs the hip examined and, if in doubt, imaged.
candidates.angle: People describe where they feel pain, not where it starts. A knee X-ray after a fall can be normal while the hip is broken, and a person with dementia may point to the wrong place or not point at all.
candidates.position: Examine the hip, and image it when in doubt, in any older person with knee or thigh pain after a fall.
claims_needing_evidence: Pain arising from the hip joint can be referred to the thigh and knee (Lesher 2008, Pain Med, descriptive study of hip joint pain referral; unsure).
Case reports describe hip fractures in older people presenting with knee pain (Hughes and Love 2018, J Prim Health Care; abstract read; case report only).
The obturator and femoral nerves supply both the hip and the knee (anatomy textbook).
The frequency of knee-only presentations is unknown; the post must not give a number.
evidence_leads: Lesher JM et al. Hip joint pain referral patterns: a descriptive study. Pain Med 2008;9:22-25 (unsure)
Hughes LD, Love G. Incidental hip fracture in an outpatient clinic: the importance of patient-centred assessment. J Prim Health Care 2018;10:176-178. doi:10.1071/HC17087 (PubMed abstract read)
Standard anatomy text (for example Gray's Anatomy) on the nerve supply of the hip and knee
candidates.opening_line_draft: An older person who falls and then complains of a sore knee may have a broken hip.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a drawn outline of a leg showing the hip joint and the areas where hip pain can be felt (groin, thigh, knee), labelled from an anatomical source, with the instruction 'Knee pain after a fall: examine the hip too'.
candidates.pause: An unexpected, memorable anatomical point.
candidates.gain: An examination habit for staff and a question for families.
candidates.follow: Short teaching points that prevent missed diagnoses.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E058 notes unwitnessed falls can hide fractures in dementia; this post is about referred knee pain as a presentation.

candidates.working_title: Sixteen weeks of home physiotherapy, and the walk to the shops
candidates.core_insight: In the US CAP trial, people still not walking in daily life months after a hip fracture received 16 weeks of home physiotherapy; only about 1 in 5 in either group could then walk 300 metres in 6 minutes, and the full training programme did not clearly beat an active control.
candidates.angle: A 'negative' trial can teach two things: the control group also had frequent home visits, so the comparison was demanding, and the low absolute recovery shows how far some people have to go. It is not evidence that exercise does not help.
candidates.position: Extended rehabilitation after hip fracture needs realistic goals and further trials; a trial that did not beat an active control is no reason to withhold exercise.
claims_needing_evidence: In CAP (210 participants, mean age 80.8, enrolled within 26 weeks of hospitalisation and not walking during daily activities), 22.9% in the training group and 17.8% in the active control group could walk 300 m or more in 6 minutes at 16 weeks, a difference that was not statistically significant (Magaziner 2019, JAMA; abstract read).

Both groups received 2 to 3 home physiotherapy visits a week for 16 weeks, nutrition advice and vitamin D, calcium and multivitamins; the control group had TENS and range-of-motion exercises (same source).
In another US trial, a home exercise programme after formal rehabilitation gave a modest improvement in physical function at 6 months (SPPB difference 0.8) (Latham 2014, JAMA; abstract read).
Wider evidence on interventions to improve mobility after hip fracture (Fairhall 2022, Cochrane; unsure).
evidence_leads: Magaziner J et al. Effect of a multicomponent home-based physical therapy intervention on ambulation after hip fracture in older adults: the CAP randomized clinical trial. JAMA 2019;322:946-956. doi:10.1001/jama.2019.12964 (PubMed abstract read)

Latham NK et al. Effect of a home-based exercise program on functional recovery following rehabilitation after hip fracture: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA 2014;311:700-708. doi:10.1001/jama.2014.469 (abstract read)

candidates.opening_line_draft: In a US trial of home physiotherapy months after a hip fracture, about [N to verify] in 5 people in each group could walk [N to verify] metres in [N to verify] minutes at the end.

candidates.working_title: What gets reported after hip fracture, and what patients want back
candidates.core_insight: A UK consensus says hip fracture trials should measure deaths, pain, daily activities, mobility (walking indoors and outdoors) and quality of life, and patients interviewed in the months after a fracture put steady walking, without falls or fear of falling, for the activities they value at the top of what they wanted back.
candidates.angle: Hospital reports lead with time to surgery, length of stay and deaths at 30 days. Patients describe recovery as steady walking to do what they value. The comparison shows which parts of recovery are rarely followed after discharge.
candidates.position: Hip fracture services should report patient-valued outcomes months after discharge, including walking outdoors and pain, alongside process and mortality measures.
claims_needing_evidence: A UK consensus core outcome set for hip fracture trials comprises mortality, pain, activities of daily living, mobility and health-related quality of life, with indoor and outdoor walking status and EQ-5D recommended as measures (Haywood 2014, Bone Joint J; abstract read).

In interviews with 31 participants (12 cognitively impaired) at 4 weeks and 4 months after hip fracture, stable mobility without falls or fear of falls for valued activities was considered most important by those who had some mobility before the fracture and could say what they valued (Griffiths 2015, BMJ Open; abstract read).
The same study concluded that no single patient-reported measure could evaluate quality of care for all patients (same source).

What UK national audits currently report, including any follow-up at around 120 days (NHFD annual report; official document, check). No Scottish Hip Fracture Audit findings to be stated or implied beyond published reports.

candidates.working_title: Mood and confidence belong in hip fracture follow-up
candidates.core_insight: Low mood and fear of falling are common in the months after a hip fracture and are linked with slower recovery, so follow-up should ask about mood and confidence as well as the wound and walking.
candidates.angle: Follow-up after hip fracture focuses on the wound, the X-ray and the walking aid. Mood and confidence shape whether a person practises walking and goes out again, and they are easy to raise if someone asks.
candidates.position: Follow-up after hip fracture should include questions about mood and fear of falling, with help offered when either persists.
claims_needing_evidence: Depressive symptoms after hip fracture took about 4 months to reach their best level in a US cohort (Magaziner 2000; abstract read).

In a US cohort of 263 people aged 60 and over after hip fracture, 17% had high fear of falling at 4 weeks that then decreased and 11% had high fear that increased by 12 weeks (Bower 2020, Int J Geriatr Psychiatry; abstract read).
Depression after hip fracture is associated with poorer functional recovery (Lenze 2007, J Am Geriatr Soc, or similar cohort; unsure).
Fear of falling is associated with poorer functional outcomes after hip fracture (systematic review, e.g. Visschedijk 2010; unsure).
evidence_leads: Magaziner J et al. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2000;55:M498-507 (abstract read)
Bower ES et al. Neuroticism predicts fear of falling after hip fracture. Int J Geriatr Psychiatry 2020;35:498-506. doi:10.1002/gps.5261 (PubMed abstract read)

Lenze EJ et al. Onset of depression in elderly persons after hip fracture: implications for prevention and early intervention of late-life depression. J Am Geriatr Soc 2007;55:81-86 (unsure; title quoted verbatim)

candidates.opening_line_draft: Follow-up after a hip fracture should ask about the wound and the walking frame, and two more things: how is your mood, and are you afraid of falling?
candidates.visual_idea: Question card: three questions for a follow-up appointment (How has your mood been? Are you avoiding walking or going out because you are afraid of falling? What would you like to be able to do again?) with a small note giving the Bower 2020 finding as natural frequencies.
candidates.pause: People recovering recognise a part of recovery that nobody asked them about.
candidates.gain: Permission, and words, to raise mood and fear at an appointment.
candidates.follow: Covers the whole person's recovery, not only the bone.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E076 describes fear of falling after a first fall as a disability and E019 covers depression and dementia; this post is about mood and confidence as part of hip fracture follow-up.
